notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Science is a systematic study of the natural world based on observation, experimentation and evidence.
  • The word science is derived from the Latin word scientia, meaning knowledge.
  • Scientific knowledge is based on evidence rather than personal belief or authority.
  • Scientific knowledge is testable.
  • Scientific explanations must be capable of being verified through observation or experiment.
  • Scientific knowledge is open to modification when new evidence becomes available.
  • Science does not claim that every conclusion is permanently final.
  • Scientific knowledge is cumulative; new discoveries build on earlier knowledge.
  • Scientific knowledge must be logically consistent.
  • Repeated observations increase the reliability of a scientific conclusion.
  • Science attempts to explain natural phenomena through natural causes.
  • Scientific knowledge is intended to be objective and independent of personal preference.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Scientific Knowledge → Observation → Evidence → Experiment → Verification

2. Scientific Temper
  • Scientific temper is an attitude of thinking rationally and examining claims through evidence.
  • Scientific temper encourages questioning rather than blind acceptance.
  • It promotes curiosity, observation, logical thinking and experimentation.
  • Scientific temper requires willingness to change an opinion when better evidence becomes available.
  • Scientific temper discourages superstition and unsupported beliefs.
  • Scientific temper does not mean rejecting a statement automatically; it means examining the available evidence.
  • Healthy scepticism is an important element of scientific temper.
  • Open-mindedness is an important scientific attitude.
  • Objectivity is an essential characteristic of scientific thinking.
  • Intellectual honesty requires a scientist to report results even when they contradict the expected outcome.
  • Scientific temper promotes problem-solving through rational methods.
  • Scientific temper is useful not only in laboratories but also in everyday decision-making.
📌 Remember

Scientific Temper → Question → Test → Evidence → Accept or Reject

3. Scientific Temper and the Indian Constitution
  • Developing scientific temper is a Fundamental Duty of every citizen of India.
  • Scientific temper is mentioned in Article 51A(h) of the Constitution of India.
  • Article 51A(h) asks citizens to develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.
  • Fundamental Duties are contained in Part IVA of the Constitution.
  • Article 51A deals with Fundamental Duties.
  • Fundamental Duties were inserted into the Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
  • The Fundamental Duties were added on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.
  • Originally, ten Fundamental Duties were introduced in 1976.
  • The eleventh Fundamental Duty was added later by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Scientific Temper → Article 51A(h) → Fundamental Duty

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Article 51A(h) → Scientific temper

Article 51A(g) → Protection of natural environment

Do not confuse the two.

4. Jawaharlal Nehru and Scientific Temper
  • Jawaharlal Nehru strongly advocated the development of scientific temper in India.
  • Nehru viewed science as an important instrument for national development.
  • He promoted scientific institutions, research laboratories and technological education in independent India.
  • The expression scientific temper became closely associated with Nehru's approach to nation-building.
  • Nehru discussed the importance of scientific thinking in The Discovery of India.
  • The Discovery of India was published in 1946.
  • Nehru believed that scientific thinking should influence social attitudes as well as technological progress.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Jawaharlal Nehru → Scientific Temper → Modern Scientific India

5. Scientific Method
  • The scientific method is a systematic procedure used to investigate scientific questions.
  • Observation is generally the starting point of a scientific investigation.
  • A scientific problem or question is identified from observations.
  • A tentative explanation is formulated as a hypothesis.
  • The hypothesis is tested through observation or experiment.
  • Experimental results are recorded as data.
  • Data are analysed to determine whether they support the hypothesis.
  • A conclusion is drawn from the analysed evidence.
  • Scientific findings should be capable of verification by others.
  • Repetition of an experiment helps establish the reliability of the result.
  • A scientific investigation may lead to modification or rejection of the original hypothesis.
  • Scientific results are generally communicated to other researchers for examination and further testing.
📌 Must-Memorise Sequence

Observation → Question → Hypothesis → Experiment → Data → Analysis → Conclusion → Verification

6. Observation
  • Observation means obtaining information about an object, event or phenomenon using the senses or scientific instruments.
  • Scientific observations should be systematic.
  • Observation may be qualitative or quantitative.
  • Qualitative observations describe characteristics without numerical measurement.
  • Quantitative observations involve numerical measurements.
  • Colour, smell and texture are examples of qualitative observations.
  • Temperature, mass, length and volume are examples of quantitative observations.
  • Instruments improve the accuracy and range of scientific observations.
  • Telescopes extend human observation to distant objects.
  • Microscopes enable observation of objects too small to be seen clearly with the naked eye.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Qualitative → Description

Quantitative → Number or measurement

7. Hypothesis
  • A hypothesis is a tentative explanation proposed for an observed phenomenon.
  • A scientific hypothesis must be testable.
  • A useful hypothesis should make predictions that can be examined.
  • Experimental evidence may support or reject a hypothesis.
  • A hypothesis is not accepted merely because it appears logical.
  • A hypothesis can be modified when new evidence becomes available.
  • A hypothesis and a scientific theory are not the same.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hypothesis → Tentative explanation → Must be tested

8. Experimentation
  • An experiment is a controlled procedure used to test a hypothesis.
  • A controlled experiment attempts to change one factor while keeping other relevant factors constant.
  • The factor deliberately changed by the experimenter is called the independent variable.
  • The factor measured as a result of the change is called the dependent variable.
  • Factors maintained constant are called controlled variables.
  • A control group provides a basis for comparison in many experiments.
  • Repeating an experiment helps identify random errors.
  • A larger number of observations generally improves the reliability of experimental conclusions.
  • Experimental procedures should be described clearly enough for other researchers to repeat them.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Independent Variable → Changed

Dependent Variable → Measured

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

The independent variable is not the result.

The dependent variable is the measured response.

9. Scientific Data
  • Data are observations or measurements collected during an investigation.
  • Scientific data may be qualitative or quantitative.
  • Raw data are the original observations or measurements collected during an investigation.
  • Data may be organised using lists, tables, graphs or charts.
  • Graphs help identify patterns and relationships in numerical data.
  • Scientific conclusions should be based on the available data.
  • Data should not be altered merely to fit an expected result.
  • Selectively using only favourable data can produce misleading conclusions.
  • Reliable scientific work requires accurate recording and transparent reporting of data.
10. Scientific Fact
  • A scientific fact is an observation that has been repeatedly confirmed.
  • Scientific facts are based on empirical evidence.
  • A fact describes something observed or measured.
  • A scientific explanation attempts to explain why or how an observed fact occurs.
  • Facts, hypotheses, theories and laws have different roles in science.
📌 Remember

Fact → Confirmed observation

Hypothesis → Testable explanation

Theory → Broad, evidence-supported explanation

Law → Describes a consistent relationship or pattern

11. Scientific Theory
  • A scientific theory is a well-supported explanation of a broad range of observations.
  • Scientific theories are supported by substantial evidence.
  • A scientific theory is more than an ordinary guess.
  • Scientific theories generate testable predictions.
  • Scientific theories may be refined when new evidence becomes available.
  • Evolution by natural selection is an example of a scientific theory.
  • Cell theory is a major biological theory.
  • Atomic theory explains the nature and behaviour of matter.
  • Germ theory explains that many diseases are caused by microorganisms.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

In everyday language, theory may mean a guess.

In science, a theory is a well-supported explanatory framework.

12. Scientific Law
  • A scientific law describes a consistent relationship observed in nature.
  • Scientific laws are often expressed mathematically.
  • Newton's laws of motion are examples of scientific laws.
  • Boyle's law describes the relationship between pressure and volume of a gas under specified conditions.
  • Ohm's law relates voltage, current and resistance under appropriate conditions.
  • A scientific law primarily describes what happens under specified conditions.
  • A scientific theory primarily provides an explanation for how or why phenomena occur.
  • A scientific theory does not become a scientific law merely after receiving more evidence.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Theory → Explanation

Law → Relationship or pattern

A theory does not automatically become a law.

13. Scientific Principle
  • A scientific principle is a basic scientific concept or rule used to explain natural phenomena.
  • Archimedes' principle deals with buoyant force.
  • Pascal's principle deals with pressure transmitted through a confined fluid.
  • Bernoulli's principle relates fluid speed and pressure.
  • Principles are frequently used to explain the operation of machines and natural processes.
14. Scientific Models
  • A scientific model is a simplified representation of an object, system or process.
  • Models help scientists understand phenomena that may be too large, too small, too complex or inaccessible for direct study.
  • A globe is a model of the Earth.
  • The atomic model represents the structure of an atom.
  • Models may be physical, conceptual or mathematical.
  • Scientific models can be modified when new observations reveal limitations in an older model.
📌 Remember

Model → Simplified representation of reality

15. Evidence in Science
  • Evidence is information used to support or challenge a scientific claim.
  • Experimental observations provide scientific evidence.
  • Measurements provide scientific evidence.
  • Repeated observations generally provide stronger support than a single observation.
  • Evidence should be relevant to the claim being examined.
  • Personal experience alone is not sufficient to establish a general scientific conclusion.
  • Anecdotal evidence is generally weaker than evidence obtained through systematic investigation.
  • Scientific conclusions are strongest when independent lines of evidence support the same explanation.
  • Extraordinary claims require strong supporting evidence.
16. Empirical Knowledge
  • Empirical knowledge is knowledge derived from observation or experience.
  • Modern science relies heavily on empirical evidence.
  • An empirical claim should be capable of being examined through observation or measurement.
  • Experimentation is an important method of obtaining empirical evidence.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Empirical → Observation + Experience + Evidence

17. Verification and Replication
  • Verification involves checking whether a result or claim is supported by evidence.
  • Replication means independently repeating a study or experiment to determine whether similar results are obtained.
  • Reproducibility increases confidence in a scientific result.
  • Results that cannot be repeated require further examination.
  • Replication helps detect accidental errors, bias and unreliable findings.
  • A single experiment is usually not sufficient to establish a major scientific conclusion.
📌 Remember

Repeatable result → Greater reliability

18. Repeatability and Reproducibility
  • Repeatability refers to obtaining similar results when measurements are repeated under the same conditions.
  • Reproducibility refers to obtaining comparable results when the work is repeated under changed conditions or by other investigators.
  • Both are important for scientific reliability.
  • A reproducible result provides stronger confidence than an isolated observation.
19. Accuracy and Precision
  • Accuracy refers to how close a measurement is to the true or accepted value.
  • Precision refers to how close repeated measurements are to one another.
  • A set of measurements can be precise without being accurate.
  • A measurement can be accurate but have limited precision.
  • Proper calibration of instruments improves measurement accuracy.
  • Repeated measurement helps assess precision.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Accuracy → Closeness to true value

Precision → Closeness of repeated values to one another

20. Error in Scientific Measurement
  • No physical measurement is absolutely free from error.
  • Random errors vary unpredictably between measurements.
  • Repeating measurements can help reduce the effect of random error.
  • Systematic errors shift measurements consistently in a particular direction.
  • Faulty calibration can produce systematic error.
  • Careful experimental design reduces measurement error.
  • Scientists generally report measurements with appropriate units and precision.
21. Objectivity
  • Objectivity means examining evidence without allowing personal preferences to determine the conclusion.
  • Scientific conclusions should depend on evidence rather than the identity of the person making the claim.
  • Objectivity requires honest reporting of observations.
  • Personal belief cannot replace experimental evidence.
  • Peer examination and replication help reduce individual bias.
22. Scientific Scepticism
  • Scientific scepticism means critically examining claims before accepting them.
  • Scepticism does not mean automatically rejecting every claim.
  • A sceptical approach asks whether adequate evidence exists.
  • Scientific claims should remain open to testing.
  • Claims that contradict well-established evidence require particularly strong supporting evidence.
📌 Remember

Scientific scepticism → Demand evidence, not automatic rejection

23. Falsifiability
  • A scientific hypothesis should be capable, in principle, of being shown false by evidence.
  • The concept of falsifiability is closely associated with philosopher Karl Popper.
  • A claim that cannot possibly be tested against evidence is difficult to treat as a scientific hypothesis.
  • Failed predictions may lead to rejection or modification of a hypothesis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Karl Popper → Falsifiability

24. Inductive Approach in Science
  • Induction involves forming a general conclusion from a number of specific observations.
  • Francis Bacon strongly advocated systematic observation and experimentation.
  • Bacon is associated with the development of the empirical and inductive approach to scientific inquiry.
  • Scientific conclusions formed inductively remain open to testing by further observations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Francis Bacon → Empiricism → Inductive Method

25. Experiment and Galileo
  • Galileo Galilei strongly promoted observation, measurement and experimentation in the study of nature.
  • Galileo's work helped establish the experimental approach in modern physical science.
  • His studies of motion challenged several older Aristotelian ideas.
  • Galileo used telescopic observations to provide evidence about astronomical phenomena.
  • His observations included mountains and craters on the Moon.
  • Galileo observed the four large moons of Jupiter now known as the Galilean satellites.
  • His observations contributed to the development of modern astronomy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Galileo → Observation + Experiment → Modern Science

26. Peer Review
  • Peer review is the evaluation of scientific work by other experts in the same field.
  • Peer review aims to identify errors, weaknesses and unsupported conclusions before publication.
  • Peer review does not guarantee that a study is correct.
  • Published scientific work may still be challenged, corrected or withdrawn when new evidence emerges.
  • Scientific knowledge advances through continued criticism and testing.
27. Correlation and Causation
  • Correlation means that two variables change in a related manner.
  • Correlation alone does not prove that one variable causes the other.
  • A third factor may influence both correlated variables.
  • Controlled experiments are especially useful for examining cause-and-effect relationships.
  • Confusing correlation with causation is a common reasoning error.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Correlation ≠ Causation

28. Bias in Scientific Investigation
  • Bias is a systematic tendency that can influence observations or conclusions.
  • Confirmation bias is the tendency to favour information that supports an existing belief.
  • Selection bias occurs when the chosen sample is not representative of the group being studied.
  • Experimental design attempts to minimise bias.
  • Blinding is used in some experiments to reduce expectation-related bias.
  • Double-blind studies help reduce bias from both participants and investigators in suitable fields such as clinical research.
29. Control and Placebo
  • A control is used as a comparison against the experimental condition.
  • A placebo is an inactive treatment designed to resemble the treatment being tested.
  • Placebos are commonly used in clinical studies.
  • A placebo group helps researchers distinguish treatment effects from psychological or other non-specific effects.
  • Placebos are not required in every scientific experiment.
30. Science and Pseudoscience
  • Pseudoscience refers to claims presented as scientific but lacking reliable scientific evidence or method.
  • Pseudoscientific claims may depend heavily on testimonials rather than controlled evidence.
  • Lack of testability is a warning sign of pseudoscience.
  • Refusal to accept contradictory evidence is inconsistent with scientific thinking.
  • Cherry-picking favourable evidence is not a sound scientific practice.
  • Scientific claims should be open to independent examination.
  • Repeated failure to reproduce a claimed effect weakens confidence in the claim.
  • Scientific temper encourages people to distinguish evidence-based knowledge from superstition and pseudoscience.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Science → Testable + Evidence + Reproducible

Pseudoscience → Unsupported + Unfalsifiable + Poor verification

31. Science and Superstition
  • Superstition is a belief or practice based on unsupported assumptions rather than demonstrated causal evidence.
  • Scientific temper encourages examination of superstitious claims through evidence.
  • Coincidence alone does not establish a cause-and-effect relationship.
  • Repeated personal anecdotes are not equivalent to controlled scientific evidence.
  • Questioning superstition is consistent with the constitutional duty to develop scientific temper and the spirit of inquiry.
32. Science and Technology
  • Science primarily seeks to understand natural phenomena.
  • Technology applies scientific knowledge to practical purposes.
  • Engineering uses scientific and mathematical principles to design systems, structures and devices.
  • Scientific discovery can lead to new technology.
  • Technological advances can also provide new tools for scientific discovery.
  • The telescope is an example of technology that greatly expanded astronomical observation.
  • The microscope transformed the study of cells and microorganisms.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Science → Knowledge and explanation

Technology → Application

Engineering → Design and problem-solving

33. Science and Society
  • Scientific knowledge contributes to agriculture, medicine, transport, communication, industry and environmental management.
  • Vaccination is an important application of scientific knowledge in public health.
  • Scientific agriculture uses improved seeds, irrigation, fertilizers, pest management and soil knowledge.
  • Weather forecasting uses observations, satellites, models and atmospheric science.
  • Scientific understanding helps in disaster prediction, preparedness and mitigation.
  • Evidence-based public policy uses reliable data and scientific assessment.
  • Scientific literacy helps citizens evaluate health, environmental and technological claims.
34. Science and Ethics
  • Scientific capability and ethical acceptability are different questions.
  • Scientific research involving humans requires ethical safeguards.
  • Informed consent is an important ethical principle in human research.
  • Research involving animals is subject to ethical and legal controls.
  • Fabrication means inventing research data.
  • Falsification means manipulating research materials, processes or data.
  • Plagiarism means presenting another person's work or ideas without proper acknowledgement.
  • Fabrication, falsification and plagiarism are forms of research misconduct.
  • Ethical science requires honesty, transparency and responsibility.
📌 Remember

FFP → Fabrication + Falsification + Plagiarism

35. Scientific Communication
  • Scientific findings are communicated through research papers, reports, conferences and scientific databases.
  • Clear communication allows other researchers to evaluate scientific claims.
  • Scientific papers commonly describe methods, observations, results and conclusions.
  • Publication allows scientific work to be examined by the wider scientific community.
  • Public communication of science is important for improving scientific literacy.
36. Scientific Literacy
  • Scientific literacy is the ability to understand and use basic scientific concepts in everyday life.
  • Scientific literacy helps people interpret evidence and evaluate claims.
  • It helps distinguish reliable information from misinformation.
  • Scientific literacy is important in decisions involving health, nutrition, environment and technology.
  • Scientific literacy does not require a person to be a professional scientist.
37. Important Scientific Attitudes
  • Curiosity encourages the search for explanations.
  • Open-mindedness allows consideration of new evidence.
  • Scepticism encourages critical examination of claims.
  • Objectivity reduces the influence of personal preference.
  • Honesty requires accurate reporting of observations.
  • Perseverance is important because experiments may require repeated attempts.
  • Creativity helps scientists develop new hypotheses and experimental methods.
  • Humility allows scientists to recognise uncertainty and limitations in their knowledge.
  • Cooperation is important because much modern scientific research is collaborative.
📌 Must-Memorise

Scientific attitude → Curiosity + Evidence + Objectivity + Scepticism + Open-mindedness + Honesty

38. Important Scientists Connected with Scientific Method
  • Aristotle emphasised systematic study of nature, although many of his scientific ideas were later revised.
  • Francis Bacon promoted empirical observation and inductive reasoning.
  • Galileo Galilei strengthened the experimental and mathematical approach to physical science.
  • René Descartes emphasised systematic doubt and rational analysis.
  • Isaac Newton combined observation, mathematics and physical laws to explain natural phenomena.
  • Karl Popper emphasised falsifiability as an important feature of scientific hypotheses.
🔗 TNPSC Key Links

Francis Bacon → Induction

Galileo → Experiment

Newton → Mathematical laws of nature

Karl Popper → Falsifiability

39. National Science Day
  • National Science Day is observed in India on 28 February every year.
  • It commemorates the discovery of the Raman Effect.
  • C. V. Raman announced the discovery of the Raman Effect on 28 February 1928.
  • The Raman Effect concerns the scattering of light and changes in wavelength associated with molecular interactions.
  • C. V. Raman received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.
  • He received the Nobel Prize for his work on the scattering of light and the discovery of the effect named after him.
  • National Science Day promotes scientific awareness and scientific temper among the public.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

28 February → National Science Day → Raman Effect → C. V. Raman

40. C. V. Raman — Important Facts
  • C. V. Raman's full name was Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman.
  • He was born on 7 November 1888 at Tiruchirappalli in present-day Tamil Nadu.
  • He discovered the Raman Effect in 1928.
  • He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.
  • He was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1954.
  • The Raman Effect is used in Raman spectroscopy to study molecular structure.
  • C. V. Raman was one of India's most internationally recognised physicists.
🔗 TNPSC Tamil Nadu Link

C. V. Raman → Born in Tiruchirappalli → Raman Effect → Nobel Prize in Physics, 1930

41. World Science Day
  • World Science Day for Peace and Development is observed on 10 November.
  • It is promoted by UNESCO.
  • The observance highlights the role of science in society and sustainable development.
  • It aims to strengthen public awareness of the importance of science.
📌 Remember

28 February → National Science Day, India

10 November → World Science Day for Peace and Development

42. Major Scientific Institutions in India
  • The Department of Science and Technology is commonly abbreviated as DST.
  • DST was established by the Government of India in 1971.
  • The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research is abbreviated as CSIR.
  • CSIR was established in 1942.
  • CSIR operates a network of national research laboratories.
  • The Indian Space Research Organisation is abbreviated as ISRO.
  • ISRO was established in 1969.
  • The Defence Research and Development Organisation is abbreviated as DRDO.
  • DRDO was formed in 1958.
  • The Indian Council of Medical Research is abbreviated as ICMR.
  • ICMR is the apex Indian body for biomedical research.
  • The Department of Atomic Energy is abbreviated as DAE.
  • The Department of Atomic Energy was established in 1954.
🔗 TNPSC Key Links

CSIR → Scientific and Industrial Research

ISRO → Space Research

DRDO → Defence Research

ICMR → Medical Research

DAE → Atomic Energy

DST → Science and Technology

43. Scientific Institutions and Personalities
  • Vikram Sarabhai is widely regarded as the father of the Indian space programme.
  • Homi J. Bhabha played a leading role in the development of India's atomic energy programme.
  • Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar was the first Director-General of CSIR.
  • The Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize is a major Indian award for scientific research.
  • A. P. J. Abdul Kalam made major contributions to India's missile and space-related programmes.
  • He is popularly known as the Missile Man of India.
🔗 TNPSC Key Links

Vikram Sarabhai → Indian Space Programme

Homi J. Bhabha → Indian Nuclear Programme

Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar → CSIR

A. P. J. Abdul Kalam → Missile Programme

44. Major Indian Science Awards and Recognition
  • The Nobel Prize is an international award given in several fields including Physics, Chemistry and Physiology or Medicine.
  • C. V. Raman received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.
  • Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1983.
  • Har Gobind Khorana shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1968.
  • Venkatraman Ramakrishnan shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009.
  • The Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize recognises outstanding scientific and technological research in India.
45. Science, Certainty and Change
  • Scientific conclusions are based on the best available evidence.
  • New evidence may modify an existing scientific explanation.
  • Revision of an explanation is a strength of science, not a weakness.
  • Uncertainty in science does not mean complete ignorance.
  • Scientists may express uncertainty using ranges, probabilities or confidence levels.
  • Strong scientific consensus develops when many independent observations support the same conclusion.
  • Scientific consensus can still change if compelling new evidence emerges.
46. Common Scientific Fallacies
  • A claim is not scientifically true merely because many people believe it.
  • A claim is not scientifically true merely because an authority states it.
  • Absence of evidence is not automatically evidence for a claim.
  • Personal experience cannot by itself establish a universal scientific rule.
  • A single exceptional case does not automatically disprove a large body of reliable evidence unless the conditions are genuinely comparable.
  • Association between two events does not necessarily establish causation.
  • Scientific reasoning requires evidence relevant to the specific claim.
47. Everyday Scientific Temper
  • Checking medicine labels and dosage instructions is an application of scientific literacy.
  • Comparing nutritional information before making a dietary claim reflects evidence-based thinking.
  • Verifying the source of a viral health claim reflects scientific temper.
  • Checking weather forecasts and official alerts before travel is an evidence-based practice.
  • Testing alternative explanations before reaching a conclusion reflects scientific thinking.
  • Asking for evidence before accepting extraordinary claims is part of scientific temper.
  • Correcting one's view after receiving better evidence is a scientific attitude.

50. TNPSC Traps
  • Scientific theory does not mean an untested guess.
  • A theory does not become a law after accumulating more evidence.
  • A law generally describes a pattern; a theory explains phenomena.
  • Correlation does not automatically establish causation.
  • Precision and accuracy are not identical.
  • Scientific scepticism does not mean rejecting everything.
  • A hypothesis must be testable.
  • A personal testimonial is not equivalent to controlled scientific evidence.
  • Replication strengthens confidence in a result.
  • Science can revise its conclusions when better evidence appears.
  • Scientific temper is a Fundamental Duty, not a Fundamental Right.
  • Article 51A(h), not Article 51A(g), deals specifically with scientific temper.
  • National Science Day is 28 February, not 28 January.
  • World Science Day is 10 November, not 28 February.
